name: Learn: Resource Quotas & Limit Ranges
objective: CKAD › Application Environment, Configuration and Security (25%). Goal: govern a namespace's resources — ResourceQuota (compute totals + object counts) and LimitRange (default and min/max per container) — and see how a quota forces pods to declare resources.
description: Namespace-level resource governance: cap total compute and object counts with ResourceQuota, and set per-container defaults and bounds with LimitRange.

questions.title: ResourceQuota — cap total compute
questions.teach:
A **ResourceQuota** limits the aggregate resources a namespace may consume. A *compute* quota (`requests.cpu`, `requests.memory`, `limits.cpu`, `limits.memory`) has a side effect worth knowing: once it exists, **every pod in that namespace must declare the matching requests/limits**, or it's rejected.

**What a quota can govern:**
- **Compute** — `requests.cpu`/`requests.memory` and `limits.cpu`/`limits.memory`. (`cpu`/`memory` without a prefix are aliases for the `requests.*` form.)
- **Extended / HugePages** — e.g. `requests.nvidia.com/gpu`, `requests.hugepages-2Mi`.
- **Object counts** — `pods`, `services`, `configmaps`, `secrets`, `persistentvolumeclaims`, plus the generic `count/<resource>.<group>` form (e.g. `count/deployments.apps`).
- **Storage** — `requests.storage`, `persistentvolumeclaims`, and per-class `<class>.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/requests.storage`.

**Ways to create one:**
- Imperative: `kubectl create quota compute-quota --hard=requests.cpu=1,limits.cpu=2,... -n <ns>`.
- Declarative YAML: `kind: ResourceQuota`, `spec.hard` map. A `spec.scopes` list (`BestEffort`, `NotBestEffort`, `Terminating`, `NotTerminating`) or `spec.scopeSelector` (needed for `PriorityClass` scopes) can restrict *which* pods the quota counts.

**Exam gotchas:**
- Once a quota constrains a compute resource, pods in that namespace **must** set the matching request/limit — a pod with no resources is rejected at admission. Pair it with a **LimitRange** so defaults are injected automatically.
- Inspect usage, not just limits, with `kubectl describe resourcequota <name> -n <ns>` (shows `Used` vs `Hard`).
- Quota is checked at admission; it does **not** retroactively evict pods already running when the quota is created.
- CPU `1` = `1000m`; memory `1Gi` (binary, 1024-based) ≠ `1G` (decimal, 1000-based).
questions.prompt:
In namespace `quota-compute`, create a ResourceQuota named `compute-quota` with hard limits: `requests.cpu=1`, `requests.memory=1Gi`, `limits.cpu=2`, `limits.memory=2Gi`.

Target: `kubectl get resourcequota compute-quota -n quota-compute` shows those hard values.

verification.description: compute-quota has the four compute hard limits

questions.title: A pod that fits under the quota
questions.teach:
Because the compute quota exists, a pod with no resources would be **rejected**. You must declare requests and limits that fit within what's left.

**How requests vs limits work:**
- **requests** = what the scheduler reserves (used for placement and for the `requests.*` quota lines). **limits** = the hard ceiling the kubelet enforces at runtime (CPU is throttled, memory over-limit is OOM-killed).
- A quota checks the *sum* across all pods. Admission fails if adding this pod would push `Used` past `Hard` for **any** tracked resource.
- Omit a limit entirely and a `limits.*` quota line will reject the pod — every constrained dimension must be present.

**Ways to declare resources:**
- Imperative `kubectl run`: use `--overrides` with a JSON `resources` block, or write YAML directly (the older `--requests/--limits` flags are removed in newer kubectl).
- Declarative YAML: a `resources:` block per container with `requests:` and `limits:` maps.
- Let a **LimitRange** inject `default`/`defaultRequest` so authors don't have to spell them out.

**Exam gotchas:**
- If a pod is rejected, read the admission error (`kubectl get events` or the apply error) — it names the exceeded quota dimension.
- Resources are **per container**; a multi-container pod's footprint is the sum of its containers (initContainers count as max, not sum).
- `requests` ≤ `limits` for each resource, or the pod is invalid.
- A Running pod still counts against the quota until it is deleted; terminating/completed pods may linger.
questions.prompt:
In `quota-compute`, create a pod `app` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) with container `requests` cpu `200m` / memory `256Mi` and `limits` cpu `500m` / memory `512Mi`. It must be admitted and reach Running.

Target: pod `app` is Running and declares those requests.
questions.hint: `kubectl run app -n quota-compute --image=busybox:1.36 --requests='cpu=200m,memory=256Mi' --limits='cpu=500m,memory=512Mi' --command -- sleep 3600` (or write YAML with a resources block).
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: quota-compute
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi}
      limits: {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
EOF

verification.description: pod 'app' is Running with resource requests set

questions.title: ResourceQuota — cap object counts
questions.teach:
A quota can also cap the **number of objects** — pods, services, configmaps, secrets, pvcs. `pods: "2"` means the namespace may hold at most two pods.

**Two ways to express object counts:**
- **Built-in names** for core resources: `pods`, `services`, `configmaps`, `secrets`, `persistentvolumeclaims`, `replicationcontrollers`, `resourcequotas`, and sub-counts like `services.loadbalancers`, `services.nodeports`.
- **Generic `count/<resource>.<group>`** for anything else, including CRDs — e.g. `count/deployments.apps`, `count/jobs.batch`, `count/cronjobs.batch`. (`count/pods` also works alongside the built-in `pods`.)

**Ways to create one:**
- Imperative: `kubectl create quota pod-quota --hard=pods=2 -n <ns>` (comma-separate multiple dimensions).
- Declarative: `kind: ResourceQuota` with a `spec.hard` map; count values are strings (`"2"`).

**Exam gotchas:**
- Counts are **current live objects**, not a cumulative total — delete a pod and the slot frees up. (Compare with Job `completions`, which is cumulative.)
- A single ResourceQuota object can mix compute, storage, and count dimensions in one `hard` map.
- Multiple ResourceQuotas in the same namespace all apply — the pod must satisfy **every** one.
- `kubectl describe quota -n <ns>` shows `Used`/`Hard` so you can see how close you are to the cap.
- Values must be quoted strings in YAML; the imperative flag takes them bare.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `quota-count`, create a ResourceQuota named `pod-quota` that limits the namespace to at most `2` pods.

Target: `pod-quota` has hard `pods: 2`.

questions.title: LimitRange — default requests & limits
questions.teach:
A **LimitRange** sets per-container policy within a namespace. With `default` (limits) and `defaultRequest` (requests), a pod that omits resources gets them **injected automatically** — handy so authors don't forget, and so a compute quota is satisfied. **The fields on a `limits[]` entry:** - `default` → the **limit** injected when a container omits limits. - `defaultRequest` → the **request** injected when a container omits requests. - `min` / `max` → the allowed bounds (rejects outside the range — see next step). - `maxLimitRequestRatio` → caps `limit/request` per resource (e.g. ratio `2` forbids a limit more than 2× the request). **The `type` of entry:** - `Container` — applies to each container (defaults + bounds). - `Pod` — bounds the **sum** across the pod (no defaulting, only min/max). - `PersistentVolumeClaim` — min/max `storage` for PVCs in the namespace. **Injection rules (the subtle part):** - Only a *missing* value is defaulted. If a container sets a request but not a limit, only the limit is injected — and vice versa. - If you set only `default` (a limit) and no `defaultRequest`, the request **inherits the limit value**. **Exam gotchas:** - LimitRange only affects pods created **after** it exists; existing pods are untouched. - Defaults are injected at admission — verify with `kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'`, not from the YAML you applied. - A LimitRange default can conflict with a `max` bound or a quota and get the pod rejected; keep them consistent. - There is no imperative `kubectl create limitrange` — write YAML (`kind: LimitRange`, `spec.limits` is a **list**).
questions.prompt:
In namespace `lr-defaults`, create a LimitRange `defaults` (type `Container`) with `defaultRequest` cpu `200m` / memory `128Mi` and `default` (limits) cpu `500m` / memory `256Mi`. Then create a pod `nodefaults` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) with **no** resources block.

Target: pod `nodefaults`'s container ends up with the defaulted requests (`cpu=200m`) and limits (`cpu=500m`).
questions.hint: Apply the LimitRange YAML (type: Container, default + defaultRequest), then `kubectl run nodefaults -n lr-defaults --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600`; check with `kubectl get pod nodefaults -n lr-defaults -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}'`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: lr-defaults
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 200m
      memory: 128Mi
    default:
      cpu: 500m
      memory: 256Mi
EOF
kubectl run nodefaults -n lr-defaults --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600

verification.description: nodefaults got defaulted requests/limits from the LimitRange

questions.title: LimitRange — min and max bounds
questions.teach:
A LimitRange can also enforce **min** and **max** per container — a pod requesting outside the range is rejected. This bounds how small or large any single container may be.

**How the bounds are checked:**
- `min` is the floor for **requests**; `max` is the ceiling for **limits**. A container whose request < `min` or whose limit > `max` is rejected at admission.
- Each resource (`cpu`, `memory`, and for PVCs `storage`) can have its own `min`/`max`.
- `maxLimitRequestRatio` adds a third constraint: `limit / request` must not exceed the ratio for that resource.

**Interaction with defaults:**
- `min`/`max` and `default`/`defaultRequest` coexist in the same entry. If a container omits values, defaults are injected **first**, then the result is bounds-checked — so a bad default can itself trip the `max`.

**`type` scope for bounds:**
- `type: Container` bounds each container individually; `type: Pod` bounds the **aggregate** across all containers; `type: PersistentVolumeClaim` bounds `storage`.

**Exam gotchas:**
- YAML quoting: `cpu: 100m` is fine, but a bare integer like `cpu: 1` should be quoted (`"1"`) to keep it a string and avoid surprises.
- Only affects pods created after the LimitRange exists; it won't fix pods already Running.
- A too-tight `min`/`max` combined with a quota or defaults is the classic way a pod silently fails to schedule — read the admission error.
- `spec.limits` is a **list**; you can stack multiple `type` entries in one LimitRange object.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `lr-minmax`, create a LimitRange `constraints` (type `Container`) with `min` cpu `100m` and `max` cpu `1`.

Target: the LimitRange has `max.cpu=1` and `min.cpu=100m`.
questions.hint: Apply a LimitRange YAML with `type: Container`, `min: {cpu: 100m}`, `max: {cpu: "1"}`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: constraints
  namespace: lr-minmax
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    min:
      cpu: 100m
    max:
      cpu: "1"
EOF

verification.description: constraints LimitRange has min/max cpu bounds
